## Solution

**Key observation.** Each factor $(1 + nx^{3^n})$ contributes either $1$ (not selecting $n$) or $nx^{3^n}$ (selecting $n$). So every subset $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,1996\}$ produces a term
$$\left(\prod_{n\in S} n\right) x^{\,e(S)}, \qquad e(S)=\sum_{n\in S}3^n.$$

**Exponents are all distinct.** The value $e(S)$ written in base $3$ has digit $1$ in position $n$ iff $n\in S$, and $0$ otherwise. Since base-$3$ representation is unique, distinct subsets give distinct exponents. Hence every exponent occurs with a single well-defined coefficient, namely $\prod_{n\in S}n$.

**Ordering the exponents.** Compare two distinct subsets $S,T$ and let $n^*=\max\{n:\mathbf{1}_{n\in S}\neq \mathbf{1}_{n\in T}\}$ be the largest position where they differ. Since
$$3^{n^*} > \sum_{n<n^*}3^n = \tfrac{3^{n^*}-1}{2},$$
the sign of $e(S)-e(T)$ is determined solely by whether $n^*\in S$. The same dominance holds for the binary value $b(S)=\sum_{n\in S}2^{n-1}$, since $2^{n^*-1}>\sum_{n<n^*}2^{n-1}=2^{n^*-1}-1$. Therefore
$$e(S)<e(T) \iff b(S)<b(T).$$

So the $j$-th smallest exponent (the term $a_jx^{k_j}$, with $j=1,2,\dots$) corresponds to the unique subset $S_j$ with $b(S_j)=j$. Equivalently, $n\in S_j$ iff bit $n-1$ of the binary expansion of $j$ equals $1$, and
$$a_j=\prod_{\substack{n\,:\,\text{bit }n-1\text{ of }j=1}} n.$$

**Computing $a_{1234}$.** Decompose $1234$ in binary:
$$1234 = 1024+128+64+16+2 = 2^{10}+2^{7}+2^{6}+2^{4}+2^{1}.$$
The set bits are at positions $10,7,6,4,1$ (zero-indexed), giving $n\in\{11,8,7,5,2\}$. Thus
$$a_{1234}=11\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot 5\cdot 2 = 88\cdot 7\cdot 5\cdot 2 = 616\cdot 5\cdot 2 = 3080\cdot 2 = 6160.$$

$$\boxed{a_{1234}=6160}$$
